questions.q: What determines the order columns appear in your results?
options: The order you list them in the SELECT clause
Alphabetical order, always
The table's internal column order, regardless of what you type
SQL Server picks a random order each time
questions.explain: Listing columns in a specific order in SELECT controls exactly how they're returned, independent of the table's own definition order.

questions.q: How do you separate multiple column names in a SELECT clause?
options: With commas
With semicolons
With the AND keyword
Each column needs its own SELECT statement
questions.explain: SELECT col1, col2, col3 — commas separate each column in the list.

questions.q: Why is SELECT * considered risky in production code?
options: If a column is added to the table later, the query's output shape changes without warning
It runs slower than naming one column at a time, always
SQL Server deprecated it
It only works with views, not tables
questions.explain: SELECT * silently picks up any new columns added to the table, which can break code expecting a fixed, known shape.

questions.q: When is SELECT * a reasonable choice?
options: While exploring a table you don't know yet
Only in stored procedures
Never — it should always be avoided
Only when the table has fewer than five columns
questions.explain: For quick, ad-hoc exploration, SELECT * is fine; the concern is production code that runs repeatedly.

questions.q: What does 'SELECT LastName, FirstName FROM Person.Person;' return, compared to 'SELECT FirstName, LastName FROM Person.Person;'?
options: The same rows and values, but with the two columns in reversed order
A completely different set of rows
An error, since column order can't be changed
Only the LastName column
questions.explain: Both queries return the same data — only the order of the two columns in the output differs.
